props.title: The Razor's Edge
props.initialSlug: A journey to the edge of self.

sections.content: **The Razor's Edge (1946)** (1946) stands as one of the most ambitious spiritual quest films of Hollywood's Golden Age. Tyrone Power delivers a career-defining performance as Larry Darrell, a WWI veteran seeking enlightenment across Europe and Asia. The film boldly adapts W. Somerset Maugham's philosophical novel, tackling themes of materialism versus spirituality that would later influence works like **Easy Rider** (1969) and **Into the Wild** (2007). Director Edmund Goulding crafts a meditative pace unusual for 1940s Hollywood, allowing the existential journey to unfold naturally against lavish production values.

sections.content: Gene Tierney's portrayal of Isabel Bradley provides the worldly counterpoint to Larry's spiritual quest, representing the materialistic society he rejects. The film's exploration of post-war disillusionment resonates with later works like **The Best Years of Our Lives** (1946) and **The Man in the Gray Flannel Suit** (1956). Clifton Webb and Anne Baxter deliver powerful supporting performances, with Baxter winning an Oscar as the tragic Sophie Nelson.

The film's depiction of Eastern spirituality, while somewhat simplified for 1940s audiences, broke new ground in Hollywood's treatment of non-Western philosophy. This paved the way for later explorations in films like **Seven Years in Tibet** (1997) and **Little Buddha** (1993). The Razor's Edge's influence can be seen in contemporary spiritual quest narratives like **Eat Pray Love** (2010) and **The Secret Life of Walter Mitty** (2013). sections.content: The film's treatment of post-war trauma and spiritual seeking feels remarkably modern, anticipating the counterculture movement by two decades. Larry's rejection of conventional success and material comfort echoes through later characters like Benjamin Braddock in **The Graduate** (1967) and Chris McCandless in **Into the Wild** (2007). The film's honest portrayal of PTSD and existential crisis was ahead of its time, especially for 1946 Hollywood.
